## DI-0301 opens: one record, five letters

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is starting something new. She's calling it **DI-0301**: a
data-integrity self-assessment that will eventually touch every system at Lakeshore that creates
or holds a record — BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software), a paper donor file still in use
at one satellite site, an aging lab instrument, the cumulative record that follows a deferred
donor across every Lakeshore location. The trigger isn't a finding. It's timing: the next AABB
(Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) reassessment cycle is on the calendar,
and nobody can rule out an FDA inspection landing before it. She wants to know, system by system,
whether Lakeshore's records would hold up to either one.

She starts small, on purpose. She pulls a single electronic record out of BECS: a completed
**donor-eligibility determination** for today's donation session — the record that says a specific
donor was accepted, on what basis, and when. She's giving it a tracking label, **DED-0458**, so
the two of you can keep referring to the same record as DI-0301 moves forward. No citations yet.
Her question, stated plainly: "If an inspector picked this exact record off the screen, would it
survive the questions they'd actually ask?"

You don't know yet. Neither does she. That's the point of starting here.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure this module exists to head off: a record that *looks* fine — present, dated,
filled in, printable — but doesn't actually prove what it claims to prove, because nobody checked
whether its underlying data and its own description of itself actually match. A record can pass a
glance and fail an inspection, and the gap between those two is exactly where data-integrity
problems live.

You already run the instincts this needs, from ITSM (IT service management) disciplines you
practice daily. **Master data management** is the discipline of knowing
where the one authoritative value for a given fact lives, instead of trusting whichever copy is in
front of you. **Data lineage** is the practice of being able to trace a value back to where it
actually came from — not where a report says it came from. **Data classification** is deciding, in
advance, which data matters enough to protect carefully. ALCOA (you'll meet the acronym properly
in a moment) is those three instincts, applied letter by letter to a single record. "Who touched
this record, and when" is lineage. "Can I actually trust this record's timestamp, or does it just
look trustworthy" is a data-quality check you'd already run on a suspicious log entry in any
ordinary IT system.

Here's where the regulated world demands more. In ordinary IT operations, a data-quality gap —
a timestamp you can't fully trust, a field whose source is murky — is a ticket. Annoying, worth
fixing, but not urgent unless something else depends on it. For a record governed by current good
manufacturing practice (CGMP, the FDA's umbrella term for the quality controls drug and biologics
manufacturing must meet), each of the five letters below is tied to an actual regulatory
requirement. A gap in any one of them isn't just messy data. It's a specific compliance exposure,
with its own citation sitting behind it — which is exactly why DI-0301 is treating DED-0458 as a
real test case, not a formality.

## The rule in plain English

**Data integrity**, for the purposes of this module, is not a vague buzzword — it's a term FDA
itself defines, in guidance it published in December 2018 called *Data Integrity and Compliance
With Drug CGMP: Questions and Answers*. That guidance is **guidance tier**: FDA's current
thinking, written in "should" language, not binding regulation. It was written for drug CGMP under
21 CFR Parts 210, 211, and 212 — not Part 606, the blood-specific regulation this curriculum has
built on from the start. It reaches Lakeshore's own records the same way 211.68 always has in this
curriculum: through 21 CFR 210.2(a)'s supplementation principle, already established in
`csv-and-becs`. One line is enough here — this guidance was written for drug manufacturing, but
210.2(a) is why its CGMP concepts reach Lakeshore's own records the same way 211.68 always has.

FDA's guidance defines data integrity as completeness, consistency, and accuracy — and says that
complete, consistent, accurate data should be five things, which spell an acronym: **ALCOA**.

- **A**ttributable — tied to a specific person or system action, not anonymous.
- **L**egible — readable, not degraded or ambiguous.
- **C**ontemporaneously recorded — captured at the time the work actually happened.
- **O**riginal or a true copy — the real record, or a verified faithful copy of it.
- **A**ccurate — correct, and actually checked to be correct.

Five letters. That's the whole acronym, as FDA's own 2018 guidance uses it.

Here's the sharpest point in this module, so get it exactly right: **FDA's guidance never uses the
term "ALCOA+."** Not once, anywhere in its text. "ALCOA+" — commonly described as ALCOA with four
more letters added (Complete, Consistent, Enduring, Available) — is real, and you'll hear it
constantly in industry conversation and from auditors trained on it. But it's **industry and
international-regulator practice**, not an FDA term, and bodies like the UK's MHRA (Medicines and
Healthcare products Regulatory Agency) are commonly associated with popularizing it. This module
doesn't cite a specific MHRA or WHO document for "ALCOA+" — none has been verified for this
curriculum — and it doesn't claim FDA has adopted or endorsed it. The tiers matter: **ALCOA is
guidance-tier, FDA's own words, from a real, cited source. "ALCOA+" is industry-practice-tier,**
described here in general terms, never attributed to FDA.

One more definition this guidance supplies, worth having before you look at DED-0458: **metadata**
is the contextual information that makes a piece of data mean anything at all. A bare number is
meaningless without it. You'll see FDA's own example below.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| FDA 2018 Data Integrity Q&A, Section III.1.a | "Section three, question one, part a" | Guidance tier. Defines "data integrity" as completeness, consistency, accuracy; names ALCOA's five letters. | The source DI-0301 pulls from to test DED-0458 letter by letter. |
| 21 CFR 210.2(a) | "Two-ten point two, paragraph a" | Regulation. Parts 211 and 600–680 "supplement, not supersede, each other." | Why a drug-CGMP guidance's ALCOA concepts reach a blood-establishment record at all — already established in `csv-and-becs`. |
| Guidance footnote 5, "attributable" group: §§ 211.101(d), 211.122, 211.186, 211.188(b)(11), 212.50(c)(10) | "the footnote behind 'attributable'" | Drug-CGMP sections FDA itself ties "attributable" back to. | Named only — these are outside this course's citation set, shown so you see ALCOA isn't an invented checklist. |
| Guidance footnote 5, "legible" group: §§ 211.180(e), 212.110(b) | "the footnote behind 'legible'" | Drug-CGMP sections tied to legibility. | Named only, same reason. |
| Guidance footnote 5, "contemporaneously recorded" group: §§ 211.100(b), 211.160(a) | "the footnote behind 'contemporaneous'" | Drug-CGMP sections requiring activities documented at the time of performance. | Named only — this is the pair behind DED-0458's trickiest test below. |
| Guidance footnote 5, "original or a true copy" group: §§ 211.180, 211.194(a) | "the footnote behind 'original or a true copy'" | Drug-CGMP sections on retaining original records or true copies. | Named only. |
| Guidance footnote 5, "accurate" group: §§ 211.22(a), 211.68, 211.188, 212.60(g) | "the footnote behind 'accurate'" | Drug-CGMP sections requiring review, checked output, and complete data. | Named only. |

## The actual text

FDA's own definition, quoted verbatim from `sources/fda-guidance/data-integrity-cgmp-qa-2018.md`
(Section III, Question 1a):

> data integrity refers to the completeness, consistency, and accuracy of data. Complete,
> consistent, and accurate data should be attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded,
> original or a true copy, and accurate (ALCOA).

Read "should," not "shall" — this is guidance, FDA's recommended way of satisfying regulations
that do use "shall," not a regulation itself. The same guidance backs that sentence with its own
footnote, which is the reason you can tell your QA — or an inspector — that ALCOA isn't a
mnemonic someone made up. It's a label FDA ties to real regulatory text, quoted verbatim:

> These characteristics are important to ensuring data integrity and are addressed throughout the
> CGMP regulations for drugs. For attributable, see §§ 211.101(d), 211.122, 211.186, 211.188(b)(11),
> and 212.50(c)(10); for legible, see §§ 211.180(e) and 212.110(b); for contemporaneously recorded
> (at the time of performance), see §§ 211.100(b) and 211.160(a); for original or a true copy, see
> §§ 211.180 and 211.194(a); and for accurate, see §§ 211.22(a), 211.68, 211.188, and 212.60(g).

Those are drug-CGMP sections, outside this course's own citation set — they're named here, not
developed, just so you see the chain from "ALCOA" back to actual regulatory requirements.

Now the metadata definition, quoted in full, including its own example:

> Metadata is the contextual information required to understand data. A data value is by itself
> meaningless without additional information about the data. Metadata is often described as data
> about data. Metadata is structured information that describes, explains, or otherwise makes it
> easier to retrieve, use, or manage data. For example, the number "23" is meaningless without
> metadata, such as an indication of the unit "mg." Among other things, metadata for a particular
> piece of data could include a date/time stamp documenting when the data were acquired, a user ID
> of the person who conducted the test or analysis that generated the data, the instrument ID used
> to acquire the data, material status data, the material identification number, and audit trails.

Notice "audit trails" sitting at the end of that list. A secure, computer-generated record of who
changed what, and when, is itself a piece of metadata — context that makes the rest of the record
trustworthy. Reviewing an audit trail in practice, and what counts as a real review versus a
rubber stamp, is next module's subject, `audit-trails-and-esignatures`. Here, just notice it's on
this list.

Last, the "systems" definition, quoted verbatim:

> The American National Standards Institute (ANSI) defines systems as people, machines, and methods
> organized to accomplish a set of specific functions. Computer or related systems can refer to
> computer hardware, software, peripheral devices, networks, cloud infrastructure, personnel, and
> associated documents (e.g., user manuals and standard operating procedures).

ANSI is the American National Standards Institute, the body FDA is quoting there. If that
definition sounds familiar, it should: it's a near-twin of
[`becs-as-a-regulated-device`'s](../../csv-and-becs/becs-as-a-regulated-device/index.qmd) own
"system" definition — hardware, software, peripherals, networks, personnel, documentation. Two
different FDA source documents, two near-identical definitions. That's not a coincidence; it's the
same CGMP systems-thinking tradition showing up twice. One line is all that callback needs — this
module doesn't re-teach that lesson.

### Running DED-0458 through ALCOA

Here's the actual exercise your QA ran. DED-0458 looks complete on screen: donor name, a unique
donor identifier, a set of screening responses, an accept determination, a timestamp, the
screener's login. Walking it through ALCOA letter by letter is where the real test happens.

**Attributable — passes.** Every field in DED-0458 traces to a specific, unique BECS login: the
screener who conducted this donor's eligibility interview, not a shared or generic account. No
login, no entry. This is a clean pass, and it's worth noticing *why* it's clean: it's provable, not
assumed. Anyone can check which individual account produced this record.

**Legible — passes.** DED-0458 lives as structured data in BECS, not handwriting that degrades or
shorthand only one person can read. Every field renders the same way for anyone who pulls the
record up. Straightforward pass.

**Contemporaneously recorded — this is the trap.** DED-0458 has a timestamp field. At a glance,
that looks like exactly what "contemporaneous" requires: the record shows when the determination
happened. But your QA asked one more question — where does that timestamp actually come from? The
answer: the workstation's own local system clock, which is not synchronized to a trusted, centrally
managed time source. Nobody has verified that workstation clock matches real time. It could be
minutes off. It could, after an uncorrected drift, be more than that. The record *claims* a time.
Nothing currently proves that claim is true. "Contemporaneous" doesn't mean "has a timestamp
field" — it means the data actually reflects when the work was performed, and that's a provable
fact, not a surface feature. DED-0458 looks like it passes. It doesn't yet.

**Original or a true copy — passes, with a nuance worth flagging.** The record your QA is
examining is the live row inside BECS's own database — the original electronic record, not a
printout or a manual re-entry of it. That's a real pass today. The nuance: if anyone later decides
to retain a printed report generated from this record instead of the underlying BECS record
itself, that question gets more complicated — whether a printout can stand in for a dynamic
electronic original is a question this curriculum picks up directly in
`predicate-rules-and-hybrid-systems`. For today's DED-0458, the original record is what's being
kept, and that's what passes.

**Accurate — open, not yet resolved.** This is the one your QA flagged as genuinely unfinished.
"Accurate" isn't just "legible and present" — it means the recorded determination actually matches
what should have resulted from the donor's actual screening answers, and that match has been
checked, not assumed. DI-0301's assessment of DED-0458 hasn't confirmed that yet one way or the
other. That's not a failure to report — an honest "still checking" is a legitimate, useful finding
for a self-assessment to produce. It's worse to call something accurate because nothing has
obviously broken than to say plainly that the check hasn't been done.

One record. Five real tests. Two clean passes, one surface-level trap, one nuance, one open
question — and that's the whole teaching point. ALCOA is something you apply to a record, not
something you read off its surface.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor wouldn't ask whether Lakeshore has an ALCOA policy. They'd ask
for specific proof, record in hand.

**For "attributable":** a list of who holds which BECS login, and confirmation no login is shared
— the same shared-credential question this curriculum has raised before, here applied to data
integrity rather than access control alone.

**For "contemporaneous":** evidence that the system clock DED-0458's timestamp came from is
actually synchronized to a trusted, centrally managed time source — not a policy saying clocks
should be accurate, but a configuration record and a log showing synchronization actually happens.
That's the systems administrator's evidence to produce, not Quality's. A bad answer sounds like
"the system shows a time, so it's contemporaneous." A good answer points to the synchronization
configuration itself.

**For "original or a true copy":** confirmation of exactly which artifact Lakeshore treats as the
record of record — the live BECS row, not whichever printed report happens to be in a binder.

**For "accurate":** evidence of an actual verification step, not an assumption that the system's
calculation is correct because nothing has visibly gone wrong.

None of this has an assigned AABB standard number in this module — if you want the adjacent
drawer, QSE 6 (Documents and Records) is the quality-system framework this ultimately feeds, not
developed further here.

## Common traps

**"FDA requires ALCOA+ compliance."** Not quite, and this is the trap worth catching before it
reaches an audit report. FDA's own 2018 guidance defines and requires attention to ALCOA — five
letters, tied to specific CGMP sections. "ALCOA+" is industry and international-regulator practice
layered on top of that, not a term FDA's guidance uses anywhere. Saying "ALCOA+" when you mean
"the five things FDA's guidance actually requires attention to" blurs a real distinction: one is
guidance tied to a citation chain; the other is useful industry vocabulary with no FDA citation
behind the "+".

**"A timestamp on a record proves it's contemporaneous."** DED-0458 is the refutation, built in.
The guidance ties "contemporaneously recorded" to activities "documented at the time of
performance" (§§ 211.100(b), 211.160(a) — named in its own footnote). A timestamp field is a
*claim* about when something happened. Whether that claim is true depends on whether the clock
that produced it can be trusted — which is a separate, checkable fact, not something a timestamp's
mere presence establishes.

## What this means for your job

- **When your QA reports a record as "passes ALCOA," ask her to walk you through all five letters,
  not give you a single pass/fail label.** DED-0458 shows why: four different answers (two passes,
  one trap, one open item) all hid behind one record that looked fine at a glance.
- **Ask specifically whether BECS workstation clocks are synchronized to a trusted, centrally
  managed time source.** You don't need to configure it yourself — you need to know whether anyone
  has verified it, and whether that verification is itself documented.
- **Correct "ALCOA+" when you hear it used as if FDA required it.** It's a useful industry term.
  It is not a citation. If a vendor or auditor says "FDA requires ALCOA+," that's worth a polite
  correction, not agreement.
- **Watch for a record's "original" status quietly shifting to a printout over time**, especially
  once people get used to working from a printed report instead of the live system record. Ask
  which one Lakeshore actually treats as authoritative, today, in writing.
- **Treat an honestly unresolved finding — like "accurate" on DED-0458 — as a good outcome of a
  self-assessment, not a bad one.** DI-0301 is doing its job if it surfaces an open question before
  an inspector does.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Someone on your team says, "FDA requires ALCOA+ compliance for all electronic records." Accurate?

Not quite — and this is worth getting exactly right. FDA's own 2018 data-integrity guidance defines
and requires attention to ALCOA: attributable, legible, contemporaneously recorded, original or a
true copy, and accurate — five letters, each tied back to specific CGMP (current good
manufacturing practice) sections in the guidance's own footnote. "ALCOA+" — commonly ALCOA plus
Complete, Consistent, Enduring, and Available — is industry and international-regulator practice,
commonly associated with bodies like the UK's MHRA, layered on top of ALCOA. It is not a term
FDA's own guidance uses anywhere in its text, and this is **not a regulatory requirement** in the
sense of being an FDA citation — it's useful industry vocabulary, not a rule FDA enforces by that
name. Tell your CIO: FDA's own guidance gives you five letters with citations behind them; "ALCOA+"
is a broader industry habit worth knowing, not an FDA rule you're failing to meet.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: DED-0458 has a timestamp showing when the donor-eligibility determination was made. Does that satisfy ALCOA's "contemporaneously recorded" element?

Not on its own. A timestamp is a claim about when something happened. DED-0458's timestamp comes
from the workstation's own local clock, which nobody has confirmed is synchronized to a trusted,
centrally managed time source. "Contemporaneously recorded" means the record actually reflects the
time the work was performed — a provable fact, backed by a trustworthy clock — not merely that a
time field exists and displays something. Until the clock's synchronization is verified, DED-0458's
timestamp is a claim, not yet a proven one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A colleague says the "systems" definition in FDA's 2018 data-integrity guidance is basically the same idea as the "system" definition in FDA's BECS validation guidance from `csv-and-becs`. Right or wrong?

Right. Both definitions describe a system as more than software: people, machines or hardware,
methods, and — in both versions — personnel and documentation, organized to accomplish specific
functions. They come from different FDA guidance documents written for different purposes, but
they rhyme because they both draw on the same CGMP systems-thinking tradition, and one (quoted
here) explicitly credits ANSI (American National Standards Institute) as its source. The parallel
is worth noticing. Neither definition needs re-teaching here — `becs-as-a-regulated-device` already
built that lesson out in full.
:::

## Where this goes next

DI-0301 has its first finding, and it's a genuinely mixed one: two clean passes, a trap that
teaches you to distrust a timestamp's surface claim, and an honest open question on "accurate."
Next, `audit-trails-and-esignatures` picks up where metadata's own list left off — audit trails —
and asks who's actually reviewing BECS's audit trail, how often, and what Lakeshore's e-signatures
would need to prove to stand in for a handwritten one.
